il_provides: A compressed on-ramp: the subset of Python that AI code actually uses, the idioms worth internalizing early, and the traps beginners hit.
OOP the way ML codebases use it: estimators, datasets, and trainers as objects with contracts — not textbook taxonomy drills.
Array thinking: the mental model under every tensor library you will touch later.
The unglamorous majority of real AI work: reshaping messy tables until a model can eat them.
Charts as instruments, not decoration: plots that reveal distribution shifts, leakage, and label errors before they become model bugs.
The statistical floor the program assumes: enough to read an evaluation table without being fooled by it.
The workflow discipline that separates a demo from a result: splits, pipelines, baselines, and reproducibility from day one.
The supervised core in the estimator vocabulary every ML library speaks: fit on train, predict on new data, regularize always.
Finding structure without labels — and the honest limits: clusters are hypotheses, not discoveries, until validated.
Just enough RL to read the literature and know where it fits — recommendation, robotics, games — and where it is overkill.
Tuning without fooling yourself: every preprocessing step inside the pipeline, inside the fold — or the scores are fiction.
The honest account of data as a scaling input: how much public text exists, what adjustments apply, and why the constraint moves — the scaling-law context behind every data decision.
One hand-worked backward pass so autograd is a tool, not magic — then the optimizers and the gradient pathologies that end training runs.
Why convolutions fit images — translation equivariance in one paragraph — and the transfer-learning workflow that makes small datasets viable.
Recurrent models taught as the bridge: powerful, finicky, and the reason the transformer was invented — which the next path takes up.
Dropout and early stopping as the program lists them — plus the discipline of tuning one thing at a time with a held-out set that stays held out.
The loop every PyTorch project shares, written by hand until it is boring: load, forward, loss, backward, step — then the engineering around it.
Attention as an operation you could implement, not a buzzword — and an honest account of scaling: capabilities grow, costs grow faster.
The architectural distinction the program's elective names: two training objectives, two task families, and why the field converged on decoders.
The pre-diffusion generative families, taught for literacy: the ideas recur in modern models, and the failure modes teach skepticism.
How diffusion models work at the level a practitioner needs — plus the honesty module: generated media as evidence of nothing but itself.
Prompting as experimental method: versioned prompts, measured outcomes, and the failure catalog (hallucination, sycophancy, instruction drift).
The production pattern behind most LLM apps: retrieve, then generate — with the cost/latency math and the cases where retrieval cannot save a bad model.
What an agent hour actually costs and how many the buildout can serve: the serving-economics lens every production agent system needs, dated honestly.
The unglamorous text work that decides whether the fancy model ever sees clean signal — and what subword tokenizers made obsolete.
From strings to vectors: the representation ladder, and why contextual embeddings ended the era of one-vector-per-word.
The classical toolkit as baselines and literacy: fast, inspectable, and still the right choice for small, well-defined text tasks.
Language modeling as the thread connecting n-grams to LSTMs to the transformer — the handoff point into the GenAI path.
The practitioner workflow: pipeline first, fine-tune second, and always read the model card before trusting a checkpoint.
Agents as control flow around a model — with the failure catalog up front, because the program's demos never show the loop that would not stop.
The two open-source poles the program names: LangChain's composition model and AutoGen's agent conversations — with guidance on when a plain loop beats both.
The low-code half of the program's Copilot module: what business users can ship in an afternoon — and the governance it needs before it touches real data.
The pro-code half: Foundry as the managed path from notebook agent to deployed service, with evaluation and safety as first-class steps.
The service catalog the exam tests: which Azure AI service answers which workload — the matching game AI-900 loves.
ML concepts in Microsoft's vocabulary: the exam tests recognition of terms and service fit, not implementation.
The principles Microsoft commits to — taught as the exam's scenario language, and as engineering obligations that outlive the exam.
The module the program lists that candidates skip: pricing, governance, and compliance are scored on AI-900 — and billed in real life.
The build discipline: baseline, error analysis, iterate — with experiments tracked so the story is tellable in an interview.
Evaluation as the proof: slices, ablations, and documented limits — the difference between a demo and evidence.
MLOps at the scale one engineer can own: a served model, monitored inputs, and a retraining plan — no platform team required.
Every capstone ships with a model card and a risk review — the habit that distinguishes an engineer from a demo artist.
The program promises a portfolio piece; this module makes it one: a repo, a story, and a demo a hiring manager can evaluate in ten minutes.
